title: Giving without a ledger
hookLine: giving, ethics, patience, effort, meditation, wisdom
carry: wisdom guides the six perfections; it keeps no ledger

cards: A gift is given. A coffee for the coworker, a ride to the airport, an afternoon helping a friend move. And then, quietly, somewhere in the back of the mind, a little ledger opens.
One for them. They owe me. Did they notice?
The gift was real. The ledger is real too. The bodhisattva, yesterday's word, sets out to help all beings, and Mahayana texts give that person six qualities to grow.
The very first one goes straight at that little ledger.

teach.b: First, the six. Paramita, a perfection: a quality practiced until it's complete. Giving.
Meditation. Wisdom. On day eight hundred eighteen you met a longer list of ten in the Jataka tradition, with its jars and stars.
Mahayana texts teach these six, and some names are shared.
Second, the first three face outward. Giving, which can be money or food, time, a teaching, or protection from fear. Ethics, keeping your conduct clean.
Patience, staying steady when someone harms you, or when life is simply hard. Third, the next three face inward. Effort, the energy that keeps you going.
Meditation, the steady, gathered mind. And wisdom, seeing that nothing, including you, is fixed and separate. Fourth, what makes them perfections.
The Diamond Sutra says, in paraphrase, that a bodhisattva should give without leaning on anything at all: not on anything seen, heard, smelled, tasted or touched.
Giving like that, the sutra says, has merit as hard to measure as space itself. No ledger.

In the Perfection of Wisdom texts, wisdom is described as the guide for the other five: without it, they're like people walking without sight, with no one to lead them to the city. With it, they find the way.
So the six aren't a ladder you climb and leave behind. Wisdom runs through each one. Giving with wisdom is giving without the ledger.
Patience with wisdom keeps no list of wrongs. That's the difference between a good deed and a perfection.

how: In Mahayana traditions the six perfections are taught as the bodhisattva's practice, and some teachers ask students to work with one at a time, beginning with giving.

o: a reward earned for doing good deeds
a quality practiced until it's complete
a rule that a bodhisattva must never break

p: time, food, a teaching, freedom from fear
the guide for the other five

s: the six perfections are a ladder you climb and leave behind
wisdom runs through each one. giving with wisdom is giving without the ledger.
the Mahayana six and the Jataka ten share some names
giving, ethics, patience, effort and wisdom appear in both lists.
in the Diamond Sutra, the perfect gift keeps careful track of who received it
a bodhisattva gives without leaning on anything at all, and the sutra calls that merit as hard to measure as space.

games.q: you've just given a friend a whole Saturday, and a little voice starts adding up what they owe you. what does the Diamond Sutra's giving ask?
o: keep the tally so it stays fair
stop giving until they pay you back
games.why: a bodhisattva gives without leaning on anything at all, and the sutra says that merit is as hard to measure as space.

practice: Let the six pass slowly, one with each out-breath: giving, ethics, patience, effort, meditation, wisdom. Go around once more and notice which one pulls at you, the one today seems to be asking for.
Then picture one moment later where it might be needed: a conversation, a chore, a line at the store.

wordCard.voice: Paramita. A perfection: giving, ethics, patience, effort, meditation and wisdom, the six qualities a bodhisattva grows, with wisdom guiding the rest. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: a perfection. the Pali form, parami, names the ten in the Jataka tradition.

carryVoice: Your line: wisdom guides the six perfections; it keeps no ledger. A gift given, and nothing counted after. See you tomorrow.
